findings.title: The claim passes into inheritance; the claimant arrives alone
findings.claim: The focus places the person's claim under divine inheritance and brings the person himself to God alone. Wider contacts make the pairing a reversal of security: 3:180 places withheld wealth under God's inheritance of heaven and earth, 19:40 names the inheritance of the earth and its inhabitants before their return, and 21:89 sets beside it the opposite plea—not to be left alone, addressed to God as best of inheritors.
findings.mechanism: The focus's inheritance verb carries what the person says into a change of title, while its coordinated coming clause makes the claimant himself the one who arrives alone. In 3:180, held wealth is joined to God's ultimate inheritance; in 19:40, divine inheritance precedes return to God; in 21:89, the same solitary state is feared by a caller asking for a successor. These contacts let the focus's transfer and solitary arrival explain one another as the loss of claimed security followed by individual presence.
findings.reader_payoff: The possessions and claim do not travel as the person's secure property, and the person who made them still arrives as an individual. The contrast with a prayer for an heir makes the solitude's stake visible without making the two situations the same.
findings.containment: The focus remains a claim about what the person says, divine inheritance, and his solitary arrival. It does not say that he withheld alms as in 3:180 or shares Zechariah's situation; the wider passages extend the relation while keeping their distinct speakers and circumstances.

findings.title: Speech, inheritance, arrival, and solitude form one sequence
findings.claim: The focus turns what the person says into the content of inheritance, then places the person himself in a coordinated arrival before God, alone. This is a transfer-and-presentation sequence: the claim's title changes, and its claimant appears without the supports he counted on. Wider connections sharpen separate parts of that sequence—wealth and offspring claims, divine inheritance, abandoned possessions and intercessors, a granted child, and the gathering of everyone—without making their speakers or events identical.
findings.mechanism: The focus analysis maps mā as the content object of inheritance, yaqulu as ongoing saying, the following wa as a coordinator joining inheritance to arrival, and fardan as the arrival's solitary condition. The contact with 34:35 makes the speech claim concrete as wealth and offspring asserted as security; 3:180 and 19:40 widen the inheritance relation to divine ownership; 6:94 joins individual arrival to abandoned gifts and claimed intercessors; 21:89–90 sets a contrary prayer for an heir beside the gift of Yahya; 2:148 places individual arrival within a universal gathering.
findings.reader_payoff: The two clauses explain one another: the thing a person claims and says passes from him, and the person himself is then brought before God. Global parallels make the sequence perceptible as one of transfer and presentation while preserving distinct local readings.
findings.containment: The focus does not name every detail in these parallels. The connections do not prove that all speakers share one story, that the focus names intercessors, or that its claimant receives the same lineage gift; they illuminate different stages without merging their circumstances.
